cards.title: A perfect copy
cards.body:
Copying how a website **looks** takes minutes: the logo, the colours, the sign-in box. What a fake site can't copy is the real **address**.

In this lesson you'll learn to read an address like a pro.

cards.title: Read the address
cards.body:
The owner of a website is the name **just before the ending** (the ending is like `.example`, `.com` or `.com.au`). These names are called [[domain names|domain-name]]. Anything after a `/` is just a page on that site.

- `yourbank.example` and `login.yourbank.example` both belong to Your Bank. `login.` in front is a [[subdomain]], and only the owner can make those.
- `yourbank.example.login-check.example` belongs to **login-check.example**: the name just before the final ending. That's the **wrong owner**.
- `yourbank-secure.example` or `yourbnak.example` are lookalikes: an extra word, or swapped letters.

cards.title: What the padlock means
cards.body:
The padlock next to an address means your connection is **encrypted** ([[HTTPS|https]]): nobody can read what you send on the way. It **doesn't** mean the site is honest. Scam sites can have a padlock too, so a padlock **only means encrypted**. (Some browsers now show a different icon there, or none at all. It still only means encrypted.)

Two more signs a sign-in page is fake:
- **Rushing you:** "Your account is locked! Sign in within 10 minutes."
- **Asks for your PIN:** a bank never asks for your card PIN on a website.

cards.prompt: Your Bank's site is `yourbank.example`. Which addresses really belong to it?
cards.explanation: Addresses ending in `yourbank.example` (with or without something like `login.` in front) are Your Bank's. `yourbank.example.login-check.example` belongs to login-check.example, and the other two are lookalikes.
cards.hint: For each one, find the ending and read the name just before it. Is that name exactly `yourbank`?
cards.nudge: Only the name just before the final ending counts. A different word, extra letters or swapped letters means a different owner.

cards.prompt: You opened this page from a link in a text. Your Bank's real site is `yourbank.example`. Tap **every** warning sign.
cards.explanation: Three warning signs: the address belongs to `login-check.example` (the **wrong owner**), the banner is **rushing you**, and it **asks for your card PIN**. The padlock and the logo look real, but they don't prove anything.
cards.hint: Read the address to find its owner. Then look for pressure, and for anything a bank would never ask for.
cards.nudge: Three things on this page match the warning signs you just learned. Look for each sign in turn.

cards.title: Safer ways in
cards.body:
- Sign in through the **official app**, a **bookmark**, or by **typing the address** yourself.
- **Don't sign in from a link** in an email or text.
- Use a [[password manager]]: it only fills in your password on the **real** site, so if it stays quiet, check the address.

Typed your details into a fake site? Change that password straight away, and tell a trusted adult. If it was a bank card, call the bank on the number on its official website or on the card.

cards.prompt: You tap a link in an email to sign in to your game account.

steps.text: The page looks right, but your **password manager doesn't offer to fill in** your password. What might that mean?

choices.text: This might not be the real site
choices.consequence: Good thinking. A password manager only fills in on the real address.

choices.text: The password manager is broken, so type it in
choices.consequence: The manager is working: it didn't recognise the address. Typing it in hands it over.

choices.text: Close the page, and open the game's app the usual way
choices.consequence: Safe. If there was really something to sign in for, you'll see it in the app.

choices.text: Type it in just once, to check
choices.consequence: Once is enough for a fake site to keep your password.

cards.explanation: A quiet password manager is a clue that the address isn't the real one. Close the page and **go there yourself**.
cards.hint: Where does a password manager fill in passwords? What's the safe way to reach an account?

cards.prompt: What does the padlock next to a web address tell you?

options.text: Your connection to the site is encrypted
The site is honest and safe
options.nudge: Scam sites can have a padlock too. Think about what the padlock actually protects.

options.text: Your bank has checked the site
options.nudge: Nobody checks a site's honesty for the padlock. It's about the connection, not the owner.

cards.explanation: The padlock means the connection is **encrypted**, so nobody can read it on the way. It says nothing about whether the site is honest.
cards.hint: Think about what HTTPS does to the data you send.

cards.prompt: Which address really belongs to Your Bank (`yourbank.example`)?

options.nudge: Find the name just before the final ending: `help-centre`. So help-centre.example owns it.
`yourbank-help` is a different name from `yourbank`: a lookalike.
`help-yourbank` isn't `yourbank`. Only the exact name before the ending counts.

cards.explanation: `help.yourbank.example` ends in `yourbank.example`, so `help.` is just a subdomain of Your Bank. The others belong to someone else.
cards.hint: For each address, find the ending, then the name just before it.

cards.prompt: Label four things on this page.
cards.explanation: The address has the **wrong owner**, the banner is **rushing you**, the page **asks for your PIN**, and the padlock **only means encrypted**: it doesn't make the site real.
cards.hint: Match each label to one part of the page. One label is about something that looks reassuring but proves nothing.
cards.nudge: Each label is something you learned about fake sign-in pages. Take one at a time and find the part it describes.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- A website's owner is the name **just before the ending** of its address.
- The **padlock only means encrypted**. Scam sites can have one.
- Warning signs: the **wrong owner**, **rushing you**, and **asking for your PIN**.
- Sign in through the **app, a bookmark or a typed address**, never from a link. A quiet password manager is a clue.

That's scams covered. Next module: keeping your private stuff private.
